title: Journaling and prayer walks
hook: evangelicals who keep prayer journals and walk their streets praying for each house

segments.voice: Yesterday, new monastics: a rule, a shared table, and neighbors at dinner. Your line was monks among us. Did you set a day? Day one thousand one hundred eighty.

A spiral notebook with a cracked cover, half full. Some pages are lists: a name, a diagnosis, a job interview, a daughter's exam. Next to a few of them, in different ink, written later, a date and one word: answered. Next to others, nothing yet. It's a prayer journal, and evangelical Christians are among those who keep them. Some of them also take the notebook in a pocket and go outside, walking their own street slowly, praying for each house they pass. Two habits, one on paper and one on foot. Today: journaling and prayer walks.

Start with the paper. When the prophet Habakkuk waits for God's answer, the answer begins: "Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it." Write it down, plainly, so it can be carried. The Psalms themselves are written prayers, complaint and praise on the same page. In one of them, the writer is so troubled he can't sleep, and then he turns: "I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old." That's what a prayer journal is for. Memory is slippery, and a page isn't. Months later you can read what you were afraid of, and see what happened, and see how your own prayers changed. Now the feet. Genesis gives Enoch one short line: "And Enoch walked with God." In that picture, a life with God is a walk. Prayer walkers borrow the picture and take it outdoors. They go slowly, eyes open, and let what they see become the prayer. A swing set: the children on this street. A for-sale sign: whoever's leaving, and whoever's coming. A wheelchair ramp. A window that stays dark. Matthew says that when Jesus went through the towns and saw the crowds, "he was moved with compassion on them." He saw first. Walking slowly is a way of seeing. Some people bring the two habits together. They walk, and then they come home and write down the houses they prayed for. And later, sometimes, they write what happened.

Here's the practice: walk your street praying. If you're able, stand up and walk, outside or slowly around the room. If you're sitting, walk your street in your mind. Go one house at a time. Notice one detail at each: a car, a toy, a porch light. Let the detail become the prayer. If you pray, you can ask God's good for whoever lives there. If you don't, simply wish them well. Keep your eyes open. The bell holds the time.
Journaling and prayer walks. Prayers written down to be remembered, and prayers walked, house by house, with eyes open.

Your line: pray as you walk. Today, on a walk you already take, to the car, the bus, the mailbox, give each house you pass one silent good word. Tonight, write one of them down. Day one thousand one hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Some evangelical Christians keep a notebook of prayer requests and note later when and how they were answered; churches and small groups also organize prayer walks, walking a neighborhood slowly and praying for the homes, schools and businesses they pass.
